Proizvolov's Identity

InvariantsCounting

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Pick half of the numbers. Sorted one way and the other, their absolute differences always add up to the same total.
How to play: Press N numbers from the pool. Watch the two columns fill, then read the sum.

Selected ↓

    Remaining ↑

      Look for the math

      No matter which half of {1, 2, …, 2N} you pick, the same total appears. That constant is N² — Proizvolov's identity.

      One small, one large in every pair

      Write the chosen numbers decreasing as a₁ > a₂ > … > aₙ and the rest increasing as b₁ < b₂ < … < bₙ. For every index i, one of aᵢ, bᵢ lies in {1, …, N} and the other in {N+1, …, 2N}. If both were small, you would have more than N distinct values below N+1; both large gives the same contradiction above N. Turn Clue on after a finish to see each pair rewritten with the larger first.

      Why the sum is N²

      Each absolute difference is then a large number minus a small one, so the whole sum is [(N+1) + … + 2N] − [1 + … + N]. That simplifies to N(2N+1) − N(N+1) = N². The logic test checks every N-subset of {1…2N} for every N from 2 to 8: the sum is always N², and every pair splits low/high.

      An invariant of the split

      The page notes a wider fact: for any set of 2N distinct numbers, if you sort one N-subset up and the complement down (or the other way around), the sum of absolute paired differences does not depend on which subset you chose. Here the set is just the first 2N naturals, so that invariant equals N².

      Set N = 4 and try two very different picks (the four largest, then four mixed). Both finished sums should read 16.
